families.label: Boosted trees
families.inductive_bias: Effects are step functions that can bend and interact; many shallow trees each correct the last.

families.label: Elastic net
families.inductive_bias: Straight-line effects shrunk toward zero; few predictors matter, correlated ones share weight.

families.label: Ridge
families.inductive_bias: Straight-line effects all shrunk toward zero together; correlated predictors share weight; none is dropped.
families.estimate: about 20 seconds, most of it tuning

families.label: Random forest
families.inductive_bias: Many deep trees, each on resampled rows with random columns, averaged; effects are step functions.
families.estimate: about 15 hours, most of it tuning

families.label: XGBoost
families.inductive_bias: Effects are step functions that can bend and interact; many shallow trees each correct the last.
families.estimate: about 1 hour, most of it tuning

families.label: Linear model
families.inductive_bias: Each predictor adds a straight-line effect; effects add up, with no interactions unless you build them.

families.label: Robust linear regression
families.inductive_bias: Straight-line effects fitted so that far-off rows count less.

families.label: Screened elastic net
concerns: With fewer features than rows the penalty alone can select; screening adds instability.
families.inductive_bias: Only features with a strong marginal association survive; among them, straight-line effects shrunk toward zero.

families.label: Random-intercept mixed model
concerns: No identifier repeats in these rows, so there is no unit for a random intercept; it is the linear model's fit.
families.inductive_bias: Straight-line effects, plus a level of its own for each unit whose rows repeat.

families.label: GEE (exchangeable)
concerns: No identifier repeats in these rows, so there is no within-unit correlation to model; it is the linear model's fit.
families.inductive_bias: Population-average straight-line or log-odds effects; a unit's rows share one correlation.

families.label: Feature-wise regression
concerns: Tests each study factor on its own and makes no predictions, so it adds nothing to a prediction.
families.inductive_bias: Each study factor tested on its own with the covariates; Benjamini–Hochberg holds the false-discovery rate.

sentences: The table was read through the `dietary` lens.
`33` cells holding `5.4e-79`, a misread SAS transport zero, were read as `0`.
`glucose` was chosen as the outcome; it is measured on all `21,849` rows.
The analysis was declared for `prediction`: models are judged on rows they never saw.
Confirmed together, each as the question showed it: `age` was confirmed to hold amounts or counts.

The model was declared for risk estimation: no classification threshold was set; performance was reported with 95% intervals within the groups of `gender`, `age`, `meds_hbp` and `meds_chol` (TRIPOD+AI 23a); no fairness method beyond that report was applied (TRIPOD+AI 14).

Column roles were set for `28` columns: energy `kcal`; covariates `age`, `gender`, `bp_sys` and 16 more; identifier `SEQN`; flags `imputed_weight`, `imputed_height`, `imputed_bmi` and 3 more; excluded `cycle_begin_year`; `bp_sys`, `bp_di` and 13 more were proposed below high confidence and wait for their own confirmation before any default reads them.
Confirmed together, each as the question showed it: `9` columns (from `bp_sys`) were confirmed as a covariate; `6` columns (from `imputed_weight`) were confirmed as a flag.
`2,270` rows with `cycle_begin_year` outside `2001`–`2015` or not recorded were excluded as the latest survey cycle, 2017–2018, is sealed whole until the final model is named (P21, emulated).

Blanks in categorical and yes/no predictors were kept as a level of their own, `Missing`; then the other predictors' missing values were imputed in each training fold without the outcome: the median for numbers, the most frequent value for categories; no row was dropped for a missing predictor.

No rows were held out; performance was estimated by internal–external validation, each level of `cycle_begin_year` held out in turn and scored by models fit on the others (seed `0`); models were compared with each other and with the no-predictor baseline on `5`-fold cross-validation repeated `10` times, by the corrected repeated k-fold t (Nadeau & Bengio 2003; Bouckaert & Frank 2004); R² was measured against the training rows' mean and pooled over every out-of-fold prediction.

The fitted models were described by their SHAP values, with their stability over 5 refits on bootstrap resamples, by a ranking of pairwise interactions (Friedman and Popescu's H statistic), and by accumulated local effects curves (Apley and Zhu 2020) of `waist`, `triglycerides`, `hdl`, `age` and `kcal`, drawn only for families whose cross-validated score beats the no-predictor baseline; these describe the models' predictions, not causal effects.

Within each training fold, every continuous predictor entered as a restricted cubic spline with its number of knots set by Harrell's rule (3 below an effective size of 30, 5 above 100, else 4) and its knots at Harrell's percentiles, so the resampling repeated each rule and its optimism is in the corrected score.
Confirmed together, each as the question showed it: `5` columns (from `kcal`) were confirmed to hold amounts or counts.

Three model families were chosen: linear regression, ridge regression and elastic net; with no rows held out, the choice among them is corrected by bootstrap bias-corrected cross-validation (Tsamardinos et al. 2018), and that selection-corrected estimate is the reported result, not the best family's own score. Read from the values, no question asked: `glucose` is a regression outcome (Continuous, with 1,575 distinct values — read as a regression outcome); `weight` is an amount (one slope) (`1,229` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `height` is an amount (one slope) (`587` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `bmi` is an amount (one slope) (`2,896` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `waist` is an amount (one slope) (`942` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `protein` is an amount (one slope) (`15,129` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `sugar` is an amount (one slope) (`17,172` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `carb` is an amount (one slope) (`18,959` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `fat_total` is an amount (one slope) (`15,355` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `fat_sat` is an amount (one slope) (`19,265` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `fat_mon` is an amount (one slope) (`19,504` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `fat_poly` is an amount (one slope) (`18,360` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `gender` is coded female female, male male (the labels spell the sexes (`female` female)); `height` is in cm (its median, 167.2, is a human height only in cm).

fit_before_opening.se_definition: Each standard error counts which rows were scored, with each fold's model as fitted (LeDell et al. 2015; DeLong's for the AUC); it leaves out how the models would vary with other training rows.

equation.text: `glucose` = 99.64 + 0.2905 × `age` + 0.04268 × `triglycerides` − 0.05705 × `sugar` + 0.2149 × `waist'` + 0.07969 × `sugar''` − 0.1962 × `hdl` − 1.909 × `age'''` + 0.1383 × `bp_sys` − 4.917 × `meds_hbp_Missing` + 3.996 × [`gender` = `male`] + 4.685 × `meds_chol_1` − 3.437 × `meds_chol_Missing` + 15 more terms; 46 coefficients shrunk to zero

explain_before_opening.methods: SHAP values were computed for a seeded sample of 1,000 of the 19,579 training rows on each model's own scale: exact linear SHAP values for the linear model, the ridge and the elastic net. Their stability was measured over 5 refits of each model on bootstrap resamples of rows, each with its own seed: the mean Spearman correlation of the inputs' mean absolute SHAP values between refits was 0.557 for the linear model, 0.482 for the ridge and 0.627 for the elastic net. The linear model, ridge and elastic net add their inputs' effects, so no interaction was found to rank. Accumulated local effects (Apley and Zhu 2020) of `waist`, `triglycerides`, `hdl`, `age` and `kcal` were drawn for each family on one grid of the inputs' quantiles, with no curve where an interval held fewer than 5 rows. These explanations describe each model's predictions, not causal effects.
relations: A family whose cross-validated score does not beat the no-predictor baseline draws no curve, and says why.
notes: Choosing predictors from these explanations and refitting is a choice made outside the cross-validation: the score would not be corrected for it.

# Methods: nhanes_prepared

_Each sentence below is the decision record's own, as it stood when this bundle was exported: answers changed before anything was seen are folded out, every change made after the held-out rows were opened is kept and marked, and a sentence that counts rows counts them as they stand. Sections follow TRIPOD+AI; a paragraph that is not the record's was written by the analysis on these answers._

## Data (TRIPOD+AI 5)

The table was read through the `dietary` lens.

## Participants (TRIPOD+AI 6)

`2,270` rows with `cycle_begin_year` outside `2001`–`2015` or not recorded were excluded as the latest survey cycle, 2017–2018, is sealed whole until the final model is named (P21, emulated).

## Data preparation (TRIPOD+AI 7)

`33` cells holding `5.4e-79`, a misread SAS transport zero, were read as `0`.

## Outcome (TRIPOD+AI 8)

`glucose` was chosen as the outcome; it is measured on all `21,849` rows.

## Predictors (TRIPOD+AI 9)

Confirmed together, each as the question showed it: `age` was confirmed to hold amounts or counts. Column roles were set for `28` columns: energy `kcal`; covariates `age`, `gender`, `bp_sys` and 16 more; identifier `SEQN`; flags `imputed_weight`, `imputed_height`, `imputed_bmi` and 3 more; excluded `cycle_begin_year`; `bp_sys`, `bp_di` and 13 more were proposed below high confidence and wait for their own confirmation before any default reads them. Confirmed together, each as the question showed it: `9` columns (from `bp_sys`) were confirmed as a covariate; `6` columns (from `imputed_weight`) were confirmed as a flag. Confirmed together, each as the question showed it: `5` columns (from `kcal`) were confirmed to hold amounts or counts.

## Missing data (TRIPOD+AI 11)

Blanks in categorical and yes/no predictors were kept as a level of their own, `Missing`; then the other predictors' missing values were imputed in each training fold without the outcome: the median for numbers, the most frequent value for categories; no row was dropped for a missing predictor.

## Analytical methods (TRIPOD+AI 12)

The analysis was declared for `prediction`: models are judged on rows they never saw. The model was declared for risk estimation: no classification threshold was set; performance was reported with 95% intervals within the groups of `gender`, `age`, `meds_hbp` and `meds_chol` (TRIPOD+AI 23a); no fairness method beyond that report was applied (TRIPOD+AI 14). No rows were held out; performance was estimated by internal–external validation, each level of `cycle_begin_year` held out in turn and scored by models fit on the others (seed `0`); models were compared with each other and with the no-predictor baseline on `5`-fold cross-validation repeated `10` times, by the corrected repeated k-fold t (Nadeau & Bengio 2003; Bouckaert & Frank 2004); R² was measured against the training rows' mean and pooled over every out-of-fold prediction. The fitted models were described by their SHAP values, with their stability over 5 refits on bootstrap resamples, by a ranking of pairwise interactions (Friedman and Popescu's H statistic), and by accumulated local effects curves (Apley and Zhu 2020) of `waist`, `triglycerides`, `hdl`, `age` and `kcal`, drawn only for families whose cross-validated score beats the no-predictor baseline; these describe the models' predictions, not causal effects. Within each training fold, every continuous predictor entered as a restricted cubic spline with its number of knots set by Harrell's rule (3 below an effective size of 30, 5 above 100, else 4) and its knots at Harrell's percentiles, so the resampling repeated each rule and its optimism is in the corrected score. Three model families were chosen: linear regression, ridge regression and elastic net; with no rows held out, the choice among them is corrected by bootstrap bias-corrected cross-validation (Tsamardinos et al. 2018), and that selection-corrected estimate is the reported result, not the best family's own score. Read from the values, no question asked: `glucose` is a regression outcome (Continuous, with 1,575 distinct values — read as a regression outcome); `weight` is an amount (one slope) (`1,229` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `height` is an amount (one slope) (`587` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `bmi` is an amount (one slope) (`2,896` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `waist` is an amount (one slope) (`942` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `protein` is an amount (one slope) (`15,129` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `sugar` is an amount (one slope) (`17,172` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `carb` is an amount (one slope) (`18,959` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `fat_total` is an amount (one slope) (`15,355` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `fat_sat` is an amount (one slope) (`19,265` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `fat_mon` is an amount (one slope) (`19,504` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `fat_poly` is an amount (one slope) (`18,360` values with decimals that fill their grid as a measurement's do (a code list's sit apart)); `gender` is coded female female, male male (the labels spell the sexes (`female` female)); `height` is in cm (its median, 167.2, is a human height only in cm).

Cross-validated R², MSE, RMSE and MAE pool every out-of-fold prediction; R² is measured against the mean of the rows each fold's model was fit on, as the held-out R² is against the training rows' mean. The fold values show the spread.

Each standard error counts which rows were scored, with each fold's model as fitted (LeDell et al. 2015; DeLong's for the AUC); it leaves out how the models would vary with other training rows.

## Reproducibility

The analysis was run in TurboTab 2.0.0.dev0 (source revision `80c1e81eea53`, with local changes). The supplementary provenance record holds the decision log (`15` records), the SHA-256 of the input file `nhanes_prepared.csv` (SHA-256 `279ed9631681`), the analysis plan (SHA-256 `472bc3a912d2`) and the model matrix (`19,579` rows by `22` columns; SHA-256 `d51dfdf251ae` as Parquet). Replaying it with `python -m turbotab.replay` checks each input file against its hash and refuses one that differs; otherwise it rebuilds the analysis from the input files and the decision log alone and compares the model matrix and every reported estimate with these.
